section.title: Adam and Christ
section.sectionRationale: Paul now lifts his argument to its widest horizon, setting the whole human race under two representative men. Through one man, Adam, sin entered the world and death spread to all, for all sinned in him. But over against Adam stands Christ, the last Adam, whose one act of righteousness brings justification and life to the many. This is the deep structure beneath everything Paul has said about justification: we were counted guilty in Adam our head, and we are counted righteous in Christ our head. The passage insists again and again that the free gift is not like the trespass, for grace superabounds, so that where sin reigned in death, grace now reigns through righteousness to eternal life. This is the theological summit of the letter's first half.
section.thesis: As sin and death came to all through the disobedience of the one man Adam, so righteousness and life come to the many through the obedience of the one man Jesus Christ; and the free gift far outstrips the trespass, so that grace reigns through righteousness to bring eternal life through our Lord.
section.frameNote: Two representative men govern the whole race: Adam, through whom sin and death entered and spread to all; and Christ, whose one act of obedience brings the abounding free gift, so that grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life. The core comparison, the gift far surpassing the trespass, is the climax of the passage.

units.label: Sin and death through one man
units.note: Adam, a pattern of the One to come

verses.text: Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, so also death was passed on to all men, because all sinned.
For sin was in the world before the law was given; but sin is not taken into account when there is no law.
Nevertheless, death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who did not sin in the way that Adam transgressed. He is a pattern of the One to come.

units.label: The free gift is not like the trespass
units.note: grace abounds all the more to the many

verses.text: But the {{charisma|gift}} is not like the trespass. For if the many died by the trespass of the one man, how much more did God’s grace and the gift that came by the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many!
Again, the gift is not like the result of the one man’s sin: The judgment that followed one sin brought condemnation, but the gift that followed many trespasses brought justification.

For if, by the trespass of the one man, death {{basileuo|reigned}} through that one man, how much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man, Jesus Christ!

units.label: Grace reigns through righteousness
units.note: one act of obedience, life for the many

verses.text: So then, just as one trespass brought condemnation for all men, so also one act of righteousness brought justification and life for all men.
For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the {{hypakoe|obedience}} of the one man the many will be made righteous.
The law came in so that the trespass would increase; but where sin increased, {{charis|grace}} increased all the more,
so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

charisma.gloss: A free gift, a gift of grace, something bestowed without cost or merit. Paul repeatedly insists the free gift is not like the trespass: whereas Adam's one sin brought condemnation, God's gift in Christ overflows to the many, answering not one sin but many trespasses. The word underlines that righteousness and life come as sheer, undeserved grace, not as anything earned.

basileuo.gloss: To reign, to rule as king. Paul personifies death, sin, and grace as reigning powers. Through Adam, death reigned over the whole race like a tyrant; but those who receive the abundance of grace will themselves reign in life through Christ, and grace reigns through righteousness to eternal life. The gospel is a change of kingdoms and of the power that rules over us.

hypakoe.gloss: Obedience, a hearing that submits. The whole passage pivots on two acts: the disobedience of Adam, by which the many were made sinners, and the obedience of Christ, by which the many will be made righteous. Christ's obedience, His whole life of submission to the Father crowned at the cross, is the one act of righteousness that grounds the believer's justification.

charis.gloss: Grace, God's undeserved favor toward sinners. Paul's climax is that where sin increased, grace increased all the more, superabounding beyond the reach of sin. Grace is not merely a divine attitude but a reigning power that triumphs over sin and death, ruling through righteousness to bring eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

basic.context: Paul has explained how sinners are justified by faith and given peace with God. Now he steps back to show the biggest picture of all: the whole human race stands under one of two men. Adam sinned, and sin and death spread to everyone. Christ obeyed, and righteousness and life come to all who are His. This is why we could be counted guilty and then counted righteous: it all turns on our representative head.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as a sustained comparison between two men, Adam and Christ, built on the pattern just as, so also. Paul keeps interrupting the comparison to insist it is not an even match: the free gift is far greater than the trespass. Follow the how much more logic. The point is not merely parallel but the overwhelming superiority of grace over sin.
basic.originalLanguages: The passage centers on the charisma, the free gift, which is not like the trespass but overflows. Paul pictures death, sin, and grace as powers that basileuo, reign, like kings. The hinge is two acts: Adam's disobedience and Christ's hypakoe, His obedience. And the summit is charis, grace, that increases all the more where sin increased and reigns to eternal life.
basic.typology: Adam is called a pattern, or type, of the One to come. He is the first head of humanity; Christ is the last Adam, the head of a new humanity. The correspondence is real but reversed: where Adam brought sin, condemnation, and death, Christ brings righteousness, justification, and life. Adam points forward by contrast to the greater Man who undoes his ruin.
basic.christ: Christ is the second and last Adam, the representative Man whose one act of obedience answers Adam's one act of disobedience. His righteousness is credited to the many so that they are made righteous, and through Him grace reigns to eternal life. Where Adam's headship brought death to all in him, Christ's headship brings life to all in Him.
basic.god: God is the giver of the free gift that far outweighs the trespass, the one whose grace superabounds beyond all sin. He is just, for condemnation follows sin, and gracious, for He provides in Christ a righteousness and life the guilty could never earn. The passage magnifies a God whose grace reigns and triumphs.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15 draws the same Adam and Christ contrast: in Adam all die, in Christ all will be made alive. Genesis 3 records the one man's trespass that Paul builds on. Romans 6 continues the theme of grace reigning without excusing sin. Philippians 2 describes Christ's obedience unto death.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's story runs from one man to one Man. Adam's fall in the garden plunged the whole race into sin and death, and every page since has groaned under that ruin. But God set another Man over a new humanity. Christ's obedience reverses Adam's disobedience, and grace, greater than all our sin, reigns through Him to eternal life.

context.literary:
The paragraph opens with 'Therefore,' tying it to Romans 5:1-11. Paul has just said that believers are justified by Christ's blood and will 'much more' be saved through His life, Romans 5:9-10. Verses 12 to 21 explain why one Man's death and life can decide the destiny of so many: because God deals with humanity through representative heads.

The grammar shows Paul thinking under pressure. Verse 12 begins 'just as,' but the matching 'so also' that should complete the comparison never arrives. Paul breaks off to answer an objection about the period before the law, verses 13 and 14, then spends verses 15 to 17 insisting on the differences between Adam and Christ before he can state the likeness. Only in verse 18 does he pick up the broken sentence: 'So then, just as... so also.' Some translations mark the break in verse 12 for this reason.

The body of the passage has a clear shape. Verses 15 to 17 give three contrasts, each marked by 'not like' or 'how much more.' Verses 18 and 19 give two balanced parallels, one about verdict, one about status. Verses 20 and 21 bring the law in and close with grace on the throne. The small word 'one' is repeated again and again, one man, one trespass, one act, because the whole argument turns on the power of a single representative act.

The language of reigning also builds deliberately. Death reigns in verses 14 and 17, sin reigns in verse 21, and grace reigns in verse 21. But in verse 17 Paul breaks the pattern: he does not say that life will reign, but that those who receive grace 'will reign in life.' Believers are not merely freed from a tyrant; they are raised to share the throne.

The closing phrase, 'through Jesus Christ our Lord,' becomes a refrain. Similar phrases close Romans 6:23, 7:25 and 8:39, so this paragraph opens the movement of chapters 6 to 8, which unfolds what life under the reign of grace means.
context.historical:
Paul wrote Romans around the middle of the first century, most likely from Corinth, commending Phoebe of nearby Cenchrea as the letter's bearer, Romans 16:1. The church in Rome included both Jewish and Gentile believers. Claudius had earlier expelled Jews from the city, Acts 18:2, and many had since returned, so tensions over the law and over who truly belonged were real. Romans 5:12-21 speaks to that tension by placing Jew and Gentile alike under one human head before placing them under another. Paul has already said that 'Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin,' Romans 3:9.

The problem of Adam was already alive in Jewish thought. The Wisdom of Solomon traced the entrance of death into the world to the envy of the devil. The apocalypse known as 4 Ezra, written after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, laments that Adam's sin was not his alone but brought ruin on all his descendants, while 2 Baruch insists that each person becomes his own Adam. Paul stands within this conversation but gives it an answer none of those writings had: a second Man whose act undoes the first.

The argument from lesser to greater, 'how much more,' was a familiar method of Jewish interpretation, and Paul uses it here as he did in Romans 5:9-10. And the language of reigning would have landed with force in the capital of an empire. In the city where Caesar ruled, Paul writes of death and sin as usurping kings, and of grace as the rightful sovereign.
context.canonical:
Paul's reading of Adam rests on Genesis. God warned that death would follow disobedience, Genesis 2:17, and the sentence 'to dust you shall return,' Genesis 3:19, is carried out in the refrain of Genesis 5, 'and then he died.' Genesis 5:3 adds that Adam fathered a son 'in his own likeness, after his own image,' so that what Adam became passes to his line. Hosea 6:7 already treats Adam's failure as covenant breaking, 'like Adam, have transgressed the covenant.'

Paul's 'the many' likely echoes Isaiah's Servant, who 'will justify many' and 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:11-12. Jesus uses the same language when He gives His life 'as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The righteous Servant whose obedience counts for others is the Old Testament root of the one act of righteousness in verse 18.

Within Paul, the closest parallel is 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 and 15:45-49, where the first man of dust and the second Man from heaven determine death and resurrection. Romans 8:29 gives the goal: to be conformed to the image of the Son, reversing the likeness inherited from Adam. Galatians 3:19 and Romans 7:7-13 fill out the brief remark of verse 20 about why the law came in. Ephesians 2:1-3 describes the same condition, 'dead in your trespasses,' 'by nature children of wrath,' from the side of personal experience.

In the history of doctrine, the passage stands at the centre of debates about original sin from Augustine and Pelagius onward, and of the Reformation teaching that the righteousness by which sinners are justified is Christ's, credited to them.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul's first aim is assurance. He has just promised that those justified will 'much more' be saved, Romans 5:9-10, and he now shows why that hope cannot fail. If one man's act could bring death to a whole race, the act of the obedient Son can certainly secure life for those who belong to Him. The comparison is meant to make believers sure.

His second aim is to level the ground between Jew and Gentile. Adam stands behind Moses. Before there was a Sinai covenant, all humanity was already under the reign of death, verse 14, so no one can claim a better standing by possessing the law, and no one is too far outside it to be reached by grace.

His third aim is to put the law in its place. It 'came in' later, verse 20, not to rescue but to expose, so that trespass would be seen for what it is and grace would be seen as greater. That sets up the objection Paul answers at once in Romans 6:1: if grace increases where sin increases, should we sin more? The passage is written so that the reader feels the scandal of grace before Paul answers it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage contains no commands. It describes what God has done in two representative men, and it describes the standing of every person in one or the other. That makes it the ground of Christian behaviour rather than instruction for it; the imperatives come in Romans 6:11-13, built on this foundation.

Its application is first a matter of self understanding. Believers should see their past in Adam honestly, without excuse, and their present in Christ confidently, without fear. It also shapes how the church speaks to the world. Because every person stands in Adam, no one is beyond the need of the gospel; because Christ's gift is 'how much more,' no one is beyond its reach. And it guards pastoral care, since those tempted to rest on their own obedience are pointed to the obedience of the one Man.

debates.question: In what sense is it true that 'all sinned,' verse 12, so that death was passed on to all?

views.label: Representative or federal headship
views.case: Adam acted as the covenant head of the race, so his one sin is counted to all he represented. This fits verses 18 and 19, where one act brings condemnation to many, and it preserves the parallel with Christ, whose one act is credited to those He represents. It also explains verse 14, where death reigned over those who had not sinned as Adam did.

views.label: Realistic or natural union
views.case: Augustine, reading the Latin 'in whom all sinned,' held that the whole race was present in Adam and truly shared his sin, inheriting both guilt and a corrupted nature. Many who do not follow his Latin text still hold that humanity sinned in Adam as its root.

views.label: Each person sins, following Adam
views.case: Others read 'because all sinned' as the personal sins of each individual. Pelagius pressed this to say that Adam's influence is only by example. Moderate forms, common in Eastern Christianity, say Adam brought death and a corrupted condition into the world, and each person, born under that power, sins in turn.

debates.bearing: The Greek phrase eph ho is best read 'because,' not 'in whom,' but the argument of verses 15 to 19 repeatedly says that the one man's act brought death and condemnation to the many. Personal sin is real, yet Paul's point is that humanity's plight was settled by a representative, just as its rescue is.

debates.question: Does 'justification and life for all men' in verse 18 mean everyone will be saved?

views.label: All who are in Christ
views.case: The two 'all men' of verse 18 match 'the many' of verse 19, and each belongs to its head. Verse 17 speaks of 'those who receive the abundance of grace,' and the whole letter teaches justification through faith, Romans 5:1. So the 'all' in Christ are all who are united to Him, drawn from every people.

views.label: Universal salvation
views.case: Some argue that the parallel must be exact: if all without exception are condemned in Adam, all without exception will be justified in Christ, and they point to Romans 11:32 and 1 Corinthians 15:22 as support.

debates.bearing: Paul's 'how much more' is about the power of the gift, not the number of its recipients. Romans 2:12 and John 3:36 show that judgment is real. The gift is sufficient for all, freely offered to all, and received by faith.

debates.question: Is the 'death' of this passage physical death, spiritual death, or both?

views.label: Physical death
views.case: Verse 14 speaks of death reigning 'from Adam until Moses,' naturally read as the mortality recorded in Genesis 5. Paul's parallel passage in 1 Corinthians 15:21-22 is about bodily death and resurrection.

views.label: The whole reality of death
views.case: The opposite of death in verses 17, 18 and 21 is 'life' and 'eternal life,' and verse 18 sets condemnation against justification. That suggests death here includes alienation from God and final judgment, as in Romans 6:23.

debates.bearing: For Paul death is one reality with many dimensions: bodily mortality is its visible sign, alienation from God its heart, and final condemnation its end. The life Christ gives answers all three, beginning with justification now and ending in the resurrection of the body, Romans 8:10-11.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 12 turns on two small words, eph ho, rendered 'because.' Augustine read the Latin translation 'in quo,' 'in whom,' and took it to mean that all sinned in Adam. Most interpreters today, including many who hold Augustine's doctrine, read the Greek as 'because' or 'inasmuch as.' Death 'was passed on,' dielthen, a verb of passing through or spreading throughout, like a contagion moving through a population.

Verse 13 says sin 'is not taken into account' where there is no law. The verb is ellogeitai, a bookkeeping term that appears in only one other place in the New Testament, Philemon 18, where Paul says of Onesimus, 'charge it to my account.' Sin was present before Moses, but it was not entered on the ledger as explicit transgression of a written command. Yet death still reigned, which shows that something deeper than personal law breaking was at work.

Adam is called a 'pattern,' typos, of the One to come. A typos is the mark left by a blow or a die, the impression that matches its stamp; Thomas uses the word for the 'nail marks' in Jesus' hands, John 20:25. Paul uses it for the wilderness events as patterns for the church, 1 Corinthians 10:6 and 10:11. Adam is the impression in the wax that shows the shape of the One who was to come.

Paul uses a whole vocabulary for what Adam did. In verse 14 it is parabasis, 'transgression,' a stepping over a known line, the word of Romans 4:15. In verses 15 to 18 it is paraptoma, 'trespass,' a false step or a fall. In verse 19 it is parakoe, 'disobedience,' formed from the verb 'to hear,' literally a mishearing or refusing to listen. Its opposite is hypakoe, obedience, a hearing under. The first man listened to the wrong voice, Genesis 3:17; the second heard and obeyed His Father.

The legal vocabulary is precise. Katakrima, 'condemnation,' in verses 16 and 18, is a sentence of judgment, and in the New Testament it appears only here and in Romans 8:1: 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.' Against it Paul sets dikaioma in verse 16, the verdict of acquittal, and uses the same word in verse 18 for Christ's 'one act of righteousness,' as though His righteous act and the righteous verdict were one. The word for 'justification' in verse 18 is dikaiosis, as in Romans 4:25, and Paul calls it literally 'justification of life.'

In verse 19 the many were 'made' sinners and will be 'made' righteous. The verb is kathistemi, 'to appoint' or 'to constitute,' used of setting someone in an office. It describes standing before God, not simply inner change. The law 'came in,' pareiselthen, a verb that can carry the sense of slipping in alongside; its relative in Galatians 2:4 describes false brothers who had 'come in under false pretenses.' The law was not an intruder, but it entered a story already under way. And 'increased all the more' is hyperperisseuo, overflowing beyond measure, the word Paul uses for joy that overflows in affliction, 2 Corinthians 7:4. Alongside charisma, Paul also calls the gift dorea and dorema, piling up words for sheer giving.

typology.type: Adam, a typos of the One to come, Romans 5:14
typology.fulfillment: A typos is the impression that shows the shape of what made it. Adam matches Christ in form: each is a single man whose act determines the standing of a whole people. Even at the moment of his fall, Adam was pointing ahead to 'the One to come.' The correspondence runs by inversion. Adam brings condemnation, Christ justification; Adam death, Christ life. The escalation is in the 'how much more': Christ does not merely cancel Adam's damage and return humanity to Eden, but gives a righteousness and a life Adam never possessed, 1 Corinthians 15:45.

Adam's act was one of refusing to hear, taking what was forbidden. Christ's act was one of submission: 'He humbled Himself and became obedient to death,' and that death was a cross, Philippians 2:8. He learned obedience through suffering, Hebrews 5:8, and bore our sins in His body on a tree, 1 Peter 2:24. Where Adam grasped at being like God, the Son who was in the form of God did not grasp but emptied Himself. Adam's act was one trespass; the gift answers 'many trespasses,' verse 16, so the answer is far greater than the offence.

typology.type: The reign of death from Adam to Moses
typology.fulfillment: Death ruled as a king over every generation, even before the law, as the funeral refrain of Genesis 5 shows. Christ answers not by making death a gentler ruler but by dethroning it: 'death no longer has dominion over Him,' Romans 6:9, and He must reign until the last enemy, death, is destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:25-26. The escalation is that His people share His reign, verse 17, 'if we endure, we will also reign with Him,' 2 Timothy 2:12, until they 'reign forever and ever,' Revelation 22:5.

typology.type: Adam's image passed to his descendants
typology.fulfillment: Adam fathered Seth 'in his own likeness, after his own image,' Genesis 5:3, so the fallen image passed down his line. In Christ a new likeness is at work: God predestined His people 'to be conformed to the image of His Son,' Romans 8:29, and 'just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man,' 1 Corinthians 15:49. The type falls short because Adam can pass on only what he is by nature; Christ gives His likeness by the Spirit to those who were not born His.

study.christ:
The passage names Christ as 'the One to come' in verse 14. Paul speaks as though, from the moment of Adam's fall, history had been waiting for someone. Luke makes a similar move when he traces Jesus' line back to 'Adam, the son of God,' Luke 3:38, and sends Him straight into the wilderness to face the tempter. Jesus is the answer to a question Genesis left open.

What Christ does is described as one act of righteousness and as His obedience. Theologians have long asked whether this means His death alone, or His whole life of obedience climaxing at the cross. Philippians 2:8 joins the two: He 'became obedient to death,' and the death was a cross. The obedience was lifelong, Hebrews 5:8, and the cross was its summit. Paul's legal vocabulary suggests that the entire righteousness of the Son is counted for His people, which is why he can say elsewhere that 'in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21.

Paul's 'the many' reaches back to Isaiah's Servant, who 'will justify many' and 'bore the sin of many,' Isaiah 53:11-12, and to Jesus' own words that He came to give His life 'as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The one act of verse 18 is the Servant's obedience to death. The 'one' is not a lonely hero but a substitute standing in the place of multitudes.

Verse 15 speaks of 'the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ.' Grace in Paul is usually God's grace, and here Paul sets 'God's grace' and the grace 'of the one man' side by side as one gift. Without making it a formula, the verse shows that the favour of God comes to us as the favour of this Man. Christ is truly human, the second representative of our race, and He is the bearer of divine grace.

The resurrection is essential to the logic. Christ 'was delivered over to death for our trespasses and was raised to life for our justification,' Romans 4:25, using the same words for trespass and justification as Romans 5:18. The verdict passed on the Son is the verdict passed on those in Him, and His risen life is the 'justification of life' they receive.

Finally, the passage shows Christ as the One through whom the reign of grace comes. He entered Adam's condition 'in the likeness of sinful man,' Romans 8:3, without Adam's sin, and tasted death 'for everyone,' Hebrews 2:9. Now death no longer rules Him, Romans 6:9, and He shares His reign with those who receive the abundance of grace.
study.god:
This passage shows God as the Lord of history who works through representatives. He did not treat humanity as billions of unconnected individuals but as a race with a head. That is a hard teaching, and readers have asked whether it is fair. Paul's answer is implicit but powerful: the same principle that brought ruin through Adam is the only principle by which rescue can come through Christ. If God could not count one man's act for many, no one could be saved by the obedience of another.

He is the Judge. The vocabulary of verses 16 and 18, judgment, condemnation, verdict, is courtroom language. God does not merely feel disappointment at sin; He passes sentence, and death is its execution. Yet the same Judge pronounces the opposite verdict, justification, on those in Christ, and does so justly, for He acts 'so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus,' Romans 3:26.

He is sovereign over the law's purpose. The law came in 'so that the trespass would increase,' verse 20, a statement of divine intention. God gave the law knowing it would expose and even provoke sin, Romans 7:7-13, because He meant to show grace as greater. Paul later says the same on the scale of the nations: 'God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone,' Romans 11:32.

His grace is asymmetrical. The 'how much more' of verses 15 and 17 is not only logic; it reflects who God is. The same pattern appears at Sinai, where His judgment reaches 'to the third and fourth generations' but His loving devotion 'to a thousand generations,' Exodus 20:5-6 and 34:6-7. God's saving purpose is always larger than His judgment.

And His grace is a king. Paul does not describe grace as a feeling in God or a mild disposition, but as a sovereign power that 'reigns through righteousness,' verse 21. Grace does not ignore justice; it rules by means of the righteousness God provides in His Son.

For worship, the passage leads where Paul himself is led in Romans 11:33-36, to wonder at the depth of God's wisdom. The right response to a God whose grace overflows beyond measure is not calculation but praise, and a life that no longer offers itself to sin, Romans 6:12-13.

crossReferences.note: God's warning that in the day Adam ate from the forbidden tree he would surely die. Paul's claim that death entered through sin, Romans 5:12, rests directly on this command and its violation. Death is not a natural part of the good creation but the announced penalty for disobedience.

Adam fathers a son in his own likeness, after his own image, and then 'he died.' The chapter repeats that refrain for generation after generation. It is the Old Testament picture of Romans 5:14, death reigning from Adam until Moses over people who never broke a written law.

Israel is charged with transgressing the covenant 'like Adam.' Hosea treats Adam's sin as covenant breaking and sees Israel repeating it. Paul's point in Romans 5:20 is similar: when the law came, Israel's trespass increased, showing that the Sinai covenant could not undo what Adam began.

The righteous Servant 'will justify many' and 'bore the sin of many.' Paul's repeated 'the many' in Romans 5:15 and 5:19 likely echoes these lines. The one man's obedience that makes many righteous is the Servant's self offering, which Paul identifies with the cross.

Jesus says the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many.' The same Servant language stands behind Romans 5, and it shows that the one act of righteousness was a death offered in the place of others, not only a good example.

The first man Adam became a living being; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. Paul adds that just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man we shall bear the likeness of the heavenly one. Romans 5 focuses on verdict and standing; this passage extends the same pattern to resurrection bodies.

Christ was delivered over for our trespasses and raised for our justification. The two key words are the same as in Romans 5:18, trespass and justification, so this verse is the hinge between chapters 4 and 5. The justifying act includes the resurrection.

Paul immediately faces the objection his own teaching invites: shall we sin more so that grace may increase? His answer, 'Certainly not!', shows that the reign of grace in Romans 5:21 is not permission but a transfer of kingdoms, from sin's rule to grace's.

Explains what Romans 5:20 means by the law coming in to increase trespass. The commandment is holy, righteous and good, but sin seizes the opportunity it gives and uses it to deceive and kill. The law exposes sin as utterly sinful; it cannot rescue from it.

'There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.' The rare word for condemnation used in Romans 5:16 and 5:18 appears here for the last time in the New Testament. The sentence passed in Adam has been lifted for all who are in the second head.

God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone. The same pattern as Romans 5:20 appears on the scale of Jews and Gentiles: God allows sin to be shown in full so that His mercy will be seen as greater, which leads Paul straight into praise.

Christ 'humbled Himself and became obedient to death,' going all the way to a cross. This is the obedience of Romans 5:19 described from inside. The Son who was in the form of God chose the path Adam refused, and His obedience ran all the way to the cross.

The servants of God 'will reign forever and ever.' This is the end of the promise in Romans 5:17 that those who receive the abundance of grace 'will reign in life.' Death's reign from Adam gives way to the reign of the redeemed with Christ in the new creation.

study.oneStory:
Romans 5:12-21 is where the whole Bible story is told in its shortest form. Creation began with a man made in God's image and set over the world to rule it, Genesis 1:26. That calling to reign is exactly what Paul has in view when he speaks of death reigning in Adam's place and believers reigning in life. Humanity was made to reign under God, and the fall handed the throne to sin and death.

The fall is not treated as one bad moment in a long history but as the event that shaped all history after it. From Adam to Moses death reigned, and the story of Genesis 5 to 11 is its proof. When the law came through Moses, it did not reverse the fall. It exposed it, and Israel's story became the fall repeated on a national scale, Hosea 6:7, ending in exile.

Redemption comes not by a better law but by a better Man. The Servant of Isaiah 53, who would justify many, and the Son of David, who would reign, meet in Jesus. His obedience, lived out and completed at the cross, and His resurrection, which declares the verdict of life, create a new humanity with a new head. The church is that new humanity, Jew and Gentile together, living now under the reign of grace even while their bodies remain mortal, Romans 8:10-11.

The passage also looks ahead. The 'eternal life' of verse 21 is life in the age to come, and the reign of believers in verse 17 is still to be completed. Paul says elsewhere that the last enemy to be destroyed is death, 1 Corinthians 15:26, and that believers will bear the likeness of the heavenly Man, 1 Corinthians 15:49.

The story ends in the new creation, where there will be no more death, Revelation 21:4, and where God's servants 'will reign forever and ever,' Revelation 22:5. What Adam was made for and lost, humanity will receive in Christ, and receive more fully than Adam ever had it, for grace always outruns the trespass.

quiz.q: How did sin and death come to the whole human race, according to verse 12?

options.text: Through one man, Adam, sin entered the world, and death spread to all because all sinned.
options.note: Adam is the representative head through whom sin and death came to all.

options.text: Each person's death is caused only by their own separate sins.
options.note: Individual sin is real, but Paul traces death to the one man Adam and the whole race in him.

options.text: Death is simply a natural part of creation with no link to sin.
options.note: Paul says death entered through sin, through the one man's trespass.

options.text: Sin came through the law of Moses.
options.note: Paul says sin was in the world before the law; death reigned from Adam until Moses.

quiz.q: Why does Paul repeat that the free gift is not like the trespass?

options.text: To show that grace in Christ far surpasses and outweighs the ruin brought by Adam.
options.note: The gift answers many trespasses and abounds all the more; grace is greater than sin.

options.text: To say Adam's sin was not really very serious.
options.note: Adam's sin was deadly serious; the point is that grace is even greater.

options.text: To teach that the gift and the trespass are exactly equal.
options.note: Paul stresses the opposite: the gift is not like the trespass but far exceeds it.

options.text: To argue that only a few are affected by Adam's sin.
options.note: The many died by the trespass; the contrast is about the surpassing greatness of grace, not a small scope.

quiz.q: What are the two acts that determine the standing of the many, in verse 19?

options.text: The disobedience of Adam and the obedience of Christ.
options.note: By one man's disobedience the many were made sinners; by the other's obedience made righteous.

options.text: Our own disobedience and our own obedience.
options.note: The passage turns on the acts of the two representative men, not our performance.

options.text: Adam's sin and our keeping of the law.
options.note: Adam's sin is right, but righteousness comes through Christ's obedience, not our law-keeping.

options.text: The obedience of Moses and the obedience of Christ.
options.note: The contrast is Adam and Christ; the law came in later and increased the trespass.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean that Adam is a pattern of the One to come?

options.text: Adam prefigures Christ as a representative head, though by contrast, since Christ reverses Adam's ruin.
options.note: Adam is a type of Christ, the last Adam, head of a new humanity.

options.text: That Adam and Christ were equally sinful men.
options.note: Christ is the obedient one whose righteousness undoes Adam's sin.

options.text: That Christ merely repeats what Adam did.
options.note: Christ does not repeat but reverses Adam's act; the correspondence is by contrast.

options.text: That Adam foreshadows Christ only in appearance, not in role.
options.note: The likeness is precisely in role, one man determining the many, though the outcomes are opposite.

quiz.q: What is the triumphant conclusion in verses 20 and 21?

options.text: Where sin increased, grace increased all the more, reigning through righteousness to eternal life.
options.note: Grace superabounds over sin and reigns to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

options.text: Since grace abounds, believers are free to keep on sinning.
options.note: Paul rejects this in Romans 6; grace reigns through righteousness, not license.

options.text: The law finally overcomes sin where grace could not.
options.note: The law increased the trespass; it is grace that superabounds and reigns.

options.text: Sin and grace remain in an equal, endless stalemate.
options.note: Grace does not merely match sin but increases all the more and reigns to eternal life.

questions: Paul says the whole race stands under one of two heads, Adam or Christ. How does understanding that your standing depends on your representative, not your own record, reshape your assurance?
The free gift is not like the trespass; grace far outweighs the ruin. Where do you need to believe that God's grace in Christ is greater than the sin that troubles you most?
Death once reigned as a tyrant, but those who receive grace will reign in life. What would it look like to live today as one who reigns in life through Christ rather than under the fear of death?
Christ's one act of obedience makes the many righteous. How does resting on His obedience, rather than trying to build your own, change the way you approach God?
Where sin increased, grace increased all the more. How can this truth guard you both from despair over your sin and from treating grace as an excuse to sin?

translationNotes.note: Because all sinned renders a phrase debated for centuries: it can mean that all sinned individually or, in context, that all sinned in Adam their representative head. The parallel with Christ, in whom the many are made righteous, favors the representative sense.

A pattern of the One to come renders the word type. Adam is a type of Christ, the correspondence being that one man's act determines the many, though Adam's act and Christ's act have opposite outcomes.

Justification and life for all men stands in parallel with the many of verse 19; read together, all men means all who are in Christ, as verse 17 limits the gift to those who receive the abundance of grace, not to every individual without exception.
